title: Full-disk encryption on a VPS: what it really protects
summary:
A search for a "privacy-focused VPS with full-disk encryption" usually ends at a checkbox on a pricing page. The checkbox is real, but what it buys you is narrower than the marketing suggests. Before you encrypt anything, it helps to be precise about who you're protecting the data from — because for one important case, disk encryption does nothing at all.

What encryption on a VPS protects — and what it doesn't

A VPS is a virtual machine on someone else's hardware. While it runs, the disk is unlocked and the encryption key lives in the VM's memory. The host machine can, in principle, read that memory. So:

Encryption helps against:

  • A copy of your disk image or snapshot ending up where it shouldn't.
  • Old drives being retired after a hardware replacement.
  • Someone getting access to storage or backups without access to your running server.

title: Why your Laravel deploy still serves the old code (and how to fix OPcache)
summary:
You ship a release. The files on the server are new. The site still behaves like the old version.

What is going on

The recommended production setting is opcache.validate_timestamps=0. PHP then never checks whether a file changed, so it keeps serving the compiled bytecode of the previous release until the process pool restarts.
The obvious fix, resetting OPcache from an Artisan command, does not work. The CLI and the FPM worker pool do not share the same OPcache, so the command resets a cache that your visitors never touch.

The fix

I built Kiln, a small package that adds four commands: kiln:clear, kiln:warm, kiln:status and kiln:config. It also adds an optional HTTP route that runs the clear or the warm inside an actual FPM worker, which is the only place that can reset the cache your site really uses.

title: Match paths the way Spring MVC does: an encoded-path bypass in API-key auth
summary:
My starter kit lets a tenant create API keys for integrations: send X-API-Key: ak_... instead of a JWT. While adding that, I made a mistake that a security review caught before the release. It's a small, common one, and the fix is one Spring Security class.

The rule: a key can't manage credentials

A key acts as the user who created it, inside the key's tenant. That's convenient, and it means a leaked key is as powerful as its creator. So a key must not be able to touch credentials or accounts. Otherwise a leaked key could mint a new key, or reset a password, and keep access after it's revoked.

The excluded areas are API keys themselves, sign-in and 2FA, the profile, and writes to users and platform administration.

AskDB is an open-source TypeScript text-to-SQL toolkit: it turns a question into checked SQL for your app to run. The model sees your schema and the notes you write, never your data.

title: How an options desk earns the right to trade real money
summary:
Strikedeck does not let a strategy touch real money until it has completed 50 paper trades at a 45 percent win rate or better, with daily loss caps and a kill switch in front of every order. Only then is the desk promoted from PAPER to LIMITED LIVE, and full LIVE still needs an operator token.

Why is gating money behind evidence a product decision?

Most trading tools treat risk controls as a settings page. The user ticks a box, and the box can be unticked at the worst possible moment. Strikedeck treats the gate as part of the product, not as an option.

The desk starts in PAPER. Every signal is logged and filled against live prices, but no order leaves the machine. The desk has to prove itself on the same data it would later trade on.

That design says something to the person using it. The software is not asking for trust up front. It asks for 50 trades of evidence first, and it shows the count on screen the whole time.

title: Deterministic Simulation Testing
summary:
Distributed systems are hard to test because partial failures overlap with live traffic and the same fault can produce different execution traces on different runs. Unmesh Joshi describes how deterministic simulation testing addresses this by replacing real clocks, networks, and storage with simulated components driven by a single-threaded execution loop. This allows simulating both hard failures and routine slowdowns—such as network and disk latency spikes—and more importantly makes every execution reproducible. This article explains the technique using a quorum key-value store as a running example, with code from Tickloom, a Java implementation of the approach.
